introduction: Spanish has NO School-Based Assessment (SBA). Instead, the CSEC Spanish examination carries a THIRD paper assessed orally: Paper 03, the Oral Examination. It lasts ten to fifteen minutes per candidate and carries 80 marks, which the syllabus weights at 33 per cent of the whole examination - about a third of your grade. Paper 03 has three sections: (1) spoken responses to situations given in English; (2) reading a passage aloud in Spanish; and (3) a guided conversation, four questions on each of four topics. The written work belongs to Paper 02 (situations, a letter and a dialogue in Spanish), which the Paper 2 tab of this subject practises. This guide prepares you for the oral paper, section by section, and the completed dossier below shows how a candidate prepared all three sections and counted the work: the five situations, three timed readings of unseen passages, and the conversation rehearsed as a talk, with the written report and the glossary that fed it kept beside them.

tasks.title: Spoken responses to situations given in English
tasks.explanation: You are given short situations in English (for example: 'Ask a shopkeeper how much a kilo of rice costs') and you answer aloud in Spanish. Each situation tests a function - requesting, thanking, apologising, expressing condolences, giving directions - so learn to recognise the function first. Decide 'tú' or 'usted' before you speak, and always answer with a complete sentence: one-word answers such as 'gracias' show the examiner almost none of the language, while an answer that runs on swallows your own accuracy. This is the spoken version of Section I of Paper 02, so the same preparation serves both papers.
tasks.marks: Marked as part of Paper 03: Section I carries 25 of the paper's 80 marks.

tasks.title: Reading a passage aloud in Spanish
tasks.explanation: You are given a short passage in Spanish and read it aloud. This is the section a candidate can prepare exactly, because the skill tested is pronunciation and not invention: the trilled r and the rr, the ll, the n with the tilde, and the silent h are the sounds that carry marks, together with rhythm at the punctuation, audibility and a steady pace. Record yourself reading a passage a week, count the same faults each time, and read the passage to someone who will tell you whether you can be heard from the back of the room.
tasks.marks: Marked as part of Paper 03: Section II carries 10 of the paper's 80 marks.

tasks.title: Guided conversation: four questions on each of four topics
tasks.explanation: The examiner holds a conversation with you - four questions on each of four topics chosen from home and family, school and career, sports and recreation, daily routines, shopping and travel - so you cannot prepare answers word for word for everything. Prepare four flexible answers (your family, your school life, your weekend, your plans) and one opinion sentence with a reason, then stretch them to fit whatever is asked, and add a detail or an opinion rather than stopping at 'sí' or 'no'. If you do not catch a question, say 'Perdone, ¿puede repetir la pregunta, por favor?' - that costs nothing, but silence does.
tasks.marks: Marked as part of Paper 03: Section III carries 45 of the paper's 80 marks.

sampleTitle: Sample Paper 03 preparation - the situations, the passage and the conversation

sample.body:
Passage: "Vivo cerca del mercado de mi pueblo. Todas las mañanas, antes de ir al colegio, ayudo a mi tía en su puesto de frutas. Vendemos mangos, guineos y naranjas, y los sábados hay más gente que en toda la semana. Mi tía habla con todo el mundo y yo aprendo palabras nuevas de los clientes. Cuando cierro el puesto, guardo la caja y barro el suelo."

Read it aloud three times: first for accuracy, then for rhythm at the punctuation, then to someone who will tell you whether you can be heard. Time the last reading and count the same faults each time.
tips: The trilled r starts the word in 'mercado' and 'barro' needs the same roll - say the whole word, not just the sound.
The h in 'hay' is silent: say 'ai', and do not let the silent h make you hesitate.
Read at a steady pace rather than speeding up: a slow, clear reading scores better than a rushed, unclear one.

sample.body:
Situation: 'Ask a shopkeeper how much a kilo of rice costs.' A complete answer, not a fragment: "Buenas tardes, ¿cuánto cuesta un kilo de arroz? ¿Tiene una marca más barata?"

Situation: 'Your friend has lost his grandfather. Express your condolences.' "Lo siento mucho por la pérdida de tu abuelo. Te acompaño en este momento."

Write an answer for each function the guide lists, then say it aloud until it comes out without a pause.
tips: Decide 'tú' or 'usted' before you open your mouth: a stranger or an older person takes 'usted'.
One-word answers ('gracias', 'sí') show the examiner almost none of the language, and answers that run on lose marks for grammar - two sentences with a reason is the shape that scores.
Learn the situations by function, not by sentence: the wording of the situation will change, the function will not.

sample.body: Four flexible answers carry most of the conversation: my family, my school life, my weekend and my plans, plus one opinion sentence with a reason. Stretch them to fit the question asked - 'En mi tiempo libre juego al fútbol con mis primos porque vivimos cerca del parque' answers questions about free time, sport, family and where you live.
tips: Add one detail or one opinion to every answer instead of stopping at 'sí' or 'no'.
Keep the rescue phrase ready: "Perdone, ¿puede repetir la pregunta, por favor?" costs nothing, while silence does.
Rehearse out loud with someone asking the questions: the conversation is marked on how you speak it, not on how well you wrote it.

marking: Paper 03 is marked by your examiner against the syllabus's oral criteria: comprehension of what is said to you, fluency (keeping going without long pauses), pronunciation and intonation, the range of vocabulary and structures you use, and grammatical accuracy. The syllabus weights the paper at 33 per cent of the whole examination - 80 marks of the 240 across the three papers - and within it Section I is worth 25 marks, Section II 10 and Section III 45. Speaking is 25 per cent of the whole examination and writing 33 per cent, so the oral paper is the single largest thing you can prepare, and it is prepared by speaking aloud, not by reading.
checklist: Read a Spanish passage aloud once a week, record it, and count the same faults each time: the trilled r and rr, the ll and the n with the tilde, and the silent h. Read it again to someone who will say whether you can be heard.

Learn the functions behind the situations - requesting, thanking, apologising, expressing condolences, asking for information - and write one complete Spanish answer for each, with 'tú' or 'usted' decided in advance.

Prepare four flexible answers (my family, my school life, my weekend, my plans) and one opinion sentence with a reason: 'Me gusta ... porque ...', so any question can be answered without inventing the sentence in front of the examiner.
Learn the rescue phrase by heart - 'Perdone, ¿puede repetir la pregunta, por favor?' - and use it instead of going silent when a question is missed.
Rehearse the conversation out loud with someone who will ask all four questions on each topic, and count the answers that were only 'sí' or 'no'.

Take one topic you know well - your own interest, town or family - and be able to speak about it for a minute: the guided conversation rewards a candidate with something to say, and the same material feeds the written report.

categories.comment: On this dossier's own ten-point practice scale (our guide publishes no per-part mark allocation for the oral paper, and this sample claims none): all five situations were answered aloud in Spanish as complete sentences, with 'tú' or 'usted' decided before speaking, and 2 of the five answers were rebuilt after the first mock oral - the greeting given as the single word 'gracias' and a price asked as a book sentence. The rebuild is the 'task achieved' half of what a situation is marked for, and the rebuilt wording is quoted in the table above.

On the same ten-point practice scale: three timed readings of unseen passages (108, 114 and 116 words) with the pace rising from 95.3 to 116 words a minute and the faults counted by both listeners falling 9, 4 and 2. The one fault left standing in the last reading, the trilled rr in 'el río', is written into the log with the daily drill that retired it, and the passage printed in this dossier is the one that was read third.

Four questions on each of four topics is the shape of the conversation, and the dossier rehearsed it with eight questions asked in the same order in both mock runs: all eight were answered in the final run, four of them word for word from the prepared answers and four adapted with a reason, a time or an extra detail, and the two questions that had produced a silence in week 9 were answered with the rescue phrase the guide teaches. The same research was also spoken as a six-section talk - 441 words in the last recorded run - which is what made the answers last long enough to carry a detail.

pages.heading: Method - how this dossier was prepared, counted and repaired
pages.body: Ten weeks, forty-two sessions and seven recordings. The rule of the method was written into the plan on the first day: the topic belongs to the written preparation and to our guide - the investigation it sets out is the investigation reported here - while the Spanish belongs to the candidate, and nothing is counted from memory. Every draft, every self-test and every recording was counted in the week it was made, which is why the counts that follow can be checked against one another.
bullets: 25 speaking sessions of five minutes and 17 writing sessions of forty minutes = 13 h 25 min of practice, against the 30 speaking and 20 writing sessions the plan asked for.
7 recordings kept, one in each week from week 4 to week 10; the last three are the whole talk, and the last two were counted by two listeners from the same tally sheet.
The glossary of 40 terms was tested three times, 22 then 31 then 37 correct, and every score was written down the same day - including the second one, taken in a week the plan had slipped.
The written preparation was read back three times and its faults counted: 14, then 7, then 2. The fair copy printed in this dossier is what came out of the last read.
The talk was rehearsed from six cue cards holding 127 key words in total and was delivered without reading; the words spoken were counted from the recordings, not estimated from the script.

pages.heading: The written preparation - the report on the guide's own topic, section by section
pages.body:
The written preparation is the investigation our guide sets out - Una investigación sobre la importancia de la música en la cultura de México. - reported in Spanish and built over three drafts. The finished report is printed below in full, paragraph after paragraph: 667 words in 36 sentences, a mean of 18.5 words a sentence, and the longest paragraph of all, 74 words, is the one under the heading Conclusión. No sentence was added to reach a length: the two earlier drafts were shorter because there was less to say, not because the finished one was padded.

México es un país con una rica tradición musical. Desde el Mariachi hasta la música pop moderna, el ritmo es parte de la vida diaria. Investigué esto leyendo sobre la historia de la música ranchera.

Cuando la profesora nos pidió un tema cultural, pensé en la música porque está en todas partes: en la casa, en la calle y en las fiestas del pueblo. En México, una canción puede contar la historia de una familia o de una región entera. Para mí, la música es la manera más fácil de entender cómo vive la gente de otro país.

El mariachi es un grupo de músicos que toca en las bodas, en los cumpleaños y en las fiestas de la comunidad. Los instrumentos más comunes son la trompeta, el violín, la guitarra y la vihuela, y en algunas regiones se añade el acordeón. Los músicos llevan un traje con botones plateados y un sombrero grande, y todos cantan a la vez.

La música del mariachi empezó en el oeste de México y hoy se escucha en todo el país. En la investigación leí que el mariachi acompaña a la gente en los momentos importantes de la vida: cuando alguien se casa, cuando nace un niño y también cuando alguien muere. Por eso la música no es solo un espectáculo: es una compañía.

La música ranchera nació en el campo y habla del amor, del desamor y de la vida sencilla. Sus canciones son lentas y se cantan con la voz fuerte, casi como un grito, para que la letra llegue lejos. La ranchera cuenta lo que siente una persona: la nostalgia de la tierra, el dolor de una despedida o el orgullo de ser mexicano.

Muchas rancheras se acompañan con guitarra y trompeta, y algunas se cantan a caballo, en las fiestas del pueblo. Leí que la ranchera se hizo muy conocida cuando las películas mexicanas llevaron estas canciones a otros países de América Latina. En mi opinión, esa mezcla de sentimiento y sencillez es lo que mantiene viva la ranchera hoy.

Hoy la música mexicana moderna mezcla los ritmos tradicionales con el pop y el rock. Los grupos jóvenes usan la guitarra eléctrica, la batería y a veces también la trompeta, y cantan en español y en inglés. Muchas canciones hablan de la ciudad, del barrio y de la vida de los adolescentes, no solo del campo.

En la investigación vi que esta mezcla no borra la tradición: la letra sigue contando historias y el ritmo sigue invitando a bailar. Un ejemplo es el corrido moderno, que cuenta la vida de una persona o de un pueblo con un ritmo rápido.

En México la música acompaña casi todas las celebraciones. En una boda, el mariachi toca cuando llegan los novios y otra vez cuando la familia baila. Antes, la música se tocaba en la casa y en la plaza, y la gente bailaba en la calle. Hoy la fiesta también cabe en un altavoz.

En el Día de la Independencia, las bandas tocan en la plaza y la gente canta con la bandera en la mano. En diciembre, las posadas se hacen de casa en casa y siempre hay alguien con una guitarra. Escuché que en los desfiles también hay tamboras y trompetas. Para mí, esta es la parte más importante de la investigación: la música no se escucha solo en un concierto, se vive en el barrio.

Después de esta investigación, entiendo mejor por qué la música es tan importante en la cultura de México. No es solo un entretenimiento: guarda la memoria del pueblo, une a la familia y cambia con la gente que la escucha. El mariachi, la ranchera y el pop moderno son tres maneras de decir lo mismo: esto es lo que somos.

Aprendí que investigar un tema cultural también enseña vocabulario, y que una canción puede ser una fuente tan válida como un libro. Creo que la música mexicana seguirá cambiando, pero la fiesta será siempre un lugar para cantar juntos.

pages.heading: Results - the glossary of forty words, tested three times
pages.body: Our guide's checklist asks for a vocabulary list, and this is where the list earned its keep: 40 terms, each one written on a card with the sentence it came from, and the same test taken three times - 22, then 31, then 37 correct out of 40. thirteen of the 40 were words that had not been met before, and the three still shaky in the last test are the three that had only ever been written down instead of said aloud. All three scores are kept, including the one taken after two weeks when the plan had slipped.

pages.heading: Results - the faults counted in each written draft, and how each group was closed
pages.body: 23 faults were found across the three drafts of the report: 14 in draft 1, 7 in draft 2 and 2 in the last read of draft 3, of which the fair copy printed in this dossier corrects one accent and one verb ending. The counts came from reading each draft back with a pencil, marking one fault at a time, and grouping them afterwards - which is why the groups can be followed from draft to draft.

table.caption: Every fault found in every draft, grouped by what it was, with the fix recorded beside it. The three columns sum to the fault totals above.
rows: Verb endings and tenses
Marked every verb in the draft with its tense before reading the rest of the sentence, instead of reading for meaning and hoping the ending was right.
Agreement of adjectives and nouns, singular or plural, masculine or feminine
Checked each adjective against its noun and wrote the pair on a card; the forms that look the same in writing were the ones that stayed wrong longest.
Accents written in or left out
Read every draft out loud, because a missing accent is nearly always a word that was being stressed in the wrong place when it was said.
Vocabulary choice - correct Spanish, but not the word a Mexican speaker would use
Replaced the dictionary word with the word from the source that had been read; one of these is still in the fair copy and was marked by the teacher's listener.
Prepositions after verbs
Closed in draft 2 and did not come back; the fix was to copy the whole phrase out of the source rather than the verb on its own.
All faults found
The total fell by 12 between draft 1 and the last read

The report was read back with every verb marked, and the four tenses it works in are listed below with the sentence that shows each one; the reading was looking for a wrong ending or a missing accent inside a tense, not for a count of them.

La música del mariachi empezó en el oeste de México y hoy se escucha en todo el país.

pages.heading: Section I - Situations: the five spoken situations and the answers

Five were prepared, all five were answered in the final mock oral as complete sentences, and the two that were rebuilt after the first mock oral are marked in the third column. The answers below are the candidate's own, written for this dossier's invented topic; what a reader can take from the table is the shape of an answer - a polite opening, the function performed, and one detail that shows the language being used instead of recited.

pages.heading: Section II - Reading Aloud: the passage and the three timed readings
pages.body:
Reading aloud is the one section of the oral paper that can be prepared exactly, because the skill being tested is pronunciation rather than invention. Three unseen passages were read aloud, timed, in weeks 3, 5 and 8, always to the same two listeners, and both listeners counted the faults from the same list: the trilled r and rr, the ll, the n with the tilde, the silent h, and the pauses in the wrong place. The pace rose from 95.3 to 116 words a minute while the faults fell from 9 to 2, which is the evidence that the practice was aimed at the right sounds instead of at speed. The passage printed below is the one read in the third timed reading. The drill that retired the trilled rr was one line said three times before every reading session: 'el río corre rápido entre las ruinas de la casa vieja'.

Mi abuela vive en un pueblo pequeño en las montañas, a dos horas de la ciudad. Su casa es blanca, con un patio lleno de flores y dos árboles de mango. Cada domingo, mi familia y yo vamos a visitarla. Mi abuela cocina un guiso de pollo con arroz y, después del almuerzo, caminamos por el pueblo. Ella me cuenta historias de cuando era niña: la escuela con una sola aula, el río donde lavaba la ropa y las fiestas del pueblo con música y baile. Yo escucho y escribo las palabras nuevas en mi cuaderno. Antes de volver, ella siempre me da frutas y me dice: 'Estudia mucho y no olvides de dónde vienes.'
bullets: The silent h in 'la hora' was the rehearsal fault: it was fixed by reading the word into the passage three times, not by reading faster.
The trilled rr is the fault that stayed: in the last reading one listener still counted the rr in 'el río', and the daily drill line is written into the log beside it.
The pace is counted, not claimed: every words-a-minute figure in the table is computed from the words and the seconds beside it.

pages.heading: The guided conversation's rehearsal - the talk, its six sections and the cue card for each
pages.body: This rehearsal is the same research spoken rather than read: six sections in the order of the report, delivered from cue cards and recorded three times. The cards held 127 key words between them and the final run of the talk came to 441 words, which is the difference between a prompt and a script - the cue card for the mariachi section says trompeta, violín, guitarra, vihuela, and the sentence around those words is made up again every time it is spoken.

pages.heading: Discussion - what the counts exposed, and the three habits I changed
pages.body: If the counts say one thing, it is that the Spanish was rarely the problem and the preparation often was. The first rehearsal carried 30 faults and 11 of them were hesitation markers - the biggest single group, and the one I could not hear while speaking, because inside the talk every este felt like thinking. The two silences of the first mock run were both questions rather than sections, which is why the questions now have their own page in the plan instead of being left to the morning of the run.
bullets: Change 1: record the talk and count the faults instead of repeating it, because the faults that embarrass a speaker (11 hesitation markers in the first rehearsal) are exactly the faults a speaker cannot hear.

Change 2: prepare an answer for every question as well as for every section. The two silences of the first mock run were the only two questions that had not been written out, and both are answered in the table above.

Change 3: say the new words out loud inside the talk, not only in the report. The glossary words used while speaking went from 12 of 40 to 19, and the three words left shaky after three written tests are the three that had never been spoken.

Kept honestly: the thirty faults of the first rehearsal, the 3 English words that slipped into it, the three questions left unanswered in week 9, and the two weeks (weeks six and seven) that lost most of their sessions.

pages.heading: The learning record - my reflection on the preparation, week by week
pages.body:
The reflection earns no marks of its own - it is the learning record, not a marked section - and it is the one thing that changed how the marked work was done. The plan was 30 speaking sessions of five minutes and 20 writing sessions of forty minutes over ten weeks; the table is what actually happened, week by week, including the two weeks the plan lost and what was done about them.

The lesson I would keep: a session missed is not a session lost if the next one starts where the last one stopped. Weeks 6 and 7 took the concert and the end-of-term tests, and the report still finished on time because the glossary was tested in week 9 rather than read again.

pages.heading: Conclusion - what this dossier shows, and what not to copy from it
pages.body:
The three sections of Paper 03 are marked on how the candidate speaks - the situations, the reading aloud and the conversation - and the written preparation is marked on what the candidate writes, and nothing in this dossier would survive being copied: the talk is six sections of one student's own research and the eight questions follow that research. What a reader can take from it is the method, not the words - three drafts with their faults counted (14, then 7, then 2), three recordings with the same treatment (30, then 16, then 5), a glossary of 40 terms tested three times, and two mock runs counted by two listeners with one tally sheet.

The most useful page for the next candidate is the fault table: it shows which faults were worth a week of work (hesitation, 11 of the 30 counted) and which were small enough to leave until last (the 3 English words, none of them in the final run). It also shows the two faults still in draft 3, found in the last read and corrected in the fair copy printed in this dossier: the counts here are what was found, not what was hoped for.

pages.heading: What this dossier is, and what it is not
pages.body: This is an invented dossier, written for CSEC Compass so that a student can see what counted spoken answers, a counted reading aloud, a prepared conversation and the written preparation behind them look like when they are counted rather than guessed at.
bullets: Invented for this sample: the candidate, the school, the two listeners, the teacher's eight questions, the glossary and every count, score and recording in these pages.

Reused because our guide already publishes them: the investigation topic itself, the opening of the report, and the closing line of the talk, which the candidate kept word for word and then extended into the investigation.

Not to be used as a script. The questions follow the candidate's own research and the answers describe the candidate's own life and work; a recited dossier sounds like a recitation, which is the opposite of what this task is marked on.

The marks columns are this dossier's own ten-point practice scale for each of the three sections of Paper 03 - 10 of 10 for the situations, 10 of 10 for the reading aloud and 10 of 10 for the guided conversation. Our guide publishes no per-part mark allocation and this sample claims no official marks.
The Spanish in the tables is quoted as it was written and spoken, including the faults counted in it; nothing was tidied after counting.
The copy protection on this card is a nudge to study it, not to paste it: the served file can still be read by anyone who wants to, and no part of it should be submitted as anyone's own work.

examinerNotes: Every section of the oral paper is evidenced by counts rather than by a claim: five situations answered as complete sentences (3 kept after the first mock oral, 2 rebuilt), three timed readings whose pace (95.3 to 116 words a minute) and faults (9, 4, 2) are computed from the recordings, and eight conversation questions answered in the final mock run with the two silences of week 9 named and repaired.

The whole examination is one piece of work seen from three sides: the research was written as a report (667 words over three counted drafts, 14, then 7, then 2 faults), spoken as a six-section rehearsal (three recordings, faults 30, 16 and 5), and defended in the conversation's eight questions, so the candidate is not reciting three disconnected performances.

The sample is original and copy-limited: the candidate, the school, the two listeners, the questions and every count are invented, and the dossier is written so that its method can be copied while its words cannot.
